abstract:
Abstract

Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

sections.body: Multimodal agents use web and image tools, but many search benchmarks use images only to identify an initial entity. The authors focus on visual context management: organizing visual information and linking it to findings during search. VisSearch-Bench contains 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains, in five categories: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, and Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. The paper notes that higher counts of image searches do not by themselves imply more complex visual context.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Some search tasks use images only to identify an entity, so the paper tests how agents link visual evidence across steps.

sections.body: This section places the benchmark among vision-language models and agentic information-seeking benchmarks such as GAIA, BrowseComp, WideSearch, and DeepSearchQA. It also reviews multimodal search benchmarks, including MMSearch, MMSearch-Plus, MM-BrowseComp, and VisBrowse-Bench. The authors argue that longer context windows do not guarantee effective visual-state management during search. Table 1 compares benchmarks on open-web access, image search, multi-image input, multi-hop reasoning, set answers, evidence links, and partial credit. VisSearch-Bench is marked as covering all listed features. In the table, no other benchmark marks set answers as covered. The comparison is qualitative and is based on task design.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: VisSearch-Bench is the only listed benchmark that covers set answers, evidence links, and partial credit together.

sections.body: Each task gives a question, an optional initial image set, and a target output format. Agents use text search, image search, reverse image search, webpage access, and image inspection. Annotators build tasks from public sources with bounded entity sets and independently verifiable fields, then write questions that hide intermediate nodes. Automated checks and human reviewers remove tasks that bypass critical visual evidence or allow a shorter unintended path. Table 2 reports 3,593 total reference-solution steps, with a median of 17.0 and a mean of 17.6 steps per task. Accuracy is 1 only when the prediction contains all and only the required content. Process Score averages, over tasks, the fraction of labeled critical states that a system recovers.
sections.heading: VisSearch-Bench
sections.headline: Each of 204 tasks is built from public sources with traceable evidence, a locked answer, and human review.

sections.body: Sixteen multimodal models are evaluated in a Direct Answer setting and with ReAct or DeerFlow agents. ReAct agents have five evidence tools: web search, webpage reading, text-based image search, reverse image search, and image cropping. Each task allows up to 30 ReAct search rounds and 60 evidence-tool calls, with a shared budget of 20 images. Results are Pass@1 from one fresh context per task. In the Direct Answer setting, no model exceeds 6.37% accuracy. The highest accuracy is 26.47%, from ReAct with Kimi-K3. ReAct with GPT-5.5 has the highest Process Score at 49.52%. In the ablation on three models, the Caption setting loses more correct answers than it gains.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Search lifts accuracy well above direct answering, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the benchmark and its results. VisSearch-Bench has 204 human-written tasks across five categories, with traceable evidence, reference answers, and scoring rules. Search improves both Accuracy and Process Score in the paired comparisons. The best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks. Model strengths vary across task categories and agent frameworks. On Set-wise Visual Search, a clear gap separates obtaining partially correct results from completing the whole task. The authors present the benchmark as a basis for measuring improvements in handling multiple images, linking clues across steps, and producing complete answers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into consistent answers remain open challenges for multimodal search agents.

sections.body: Appendix A summarizes MMSearch, MMSearch-Plus, MM-BrowseComp, and VisBrowse-Bench, and Table S1 gives their question counts and metrics. Appendix B gives prompt design: agents receive only the public question and initial images, and judging runs in separate calls for Accuracy and Process Score. Appendix C lists hyperparameters, such as a maximum image side of 1,536 px, a maximum of 20 total images, and a maximum of 30 ReAct search rounds. Appendix D describes the Pass@1 evaluation algorithm. Appendix E covers the nine release fields and the construction and release checks. Appendix F presents 17 trajectories, seven successful and ten failed, across the five task categories.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists related benchmark details, prompts, hyperparameters, release fields, and seventeen case-study trajectories.
